doc.title: Onaje Allan Gumbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001

title: High school Latin band and mentor Leroy Kirkland
summary: At Music and Art he plays in a Cal Tjader-style Latin band and is mentored by Leroy Kirkland, who introduces him to studio players.

venues.name: High School of Music and Art

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: realizing that I’d like to be a part of all this kind of music. So to shuttle between different styles of music was not a big thing for me, through high school I was playing with a Latin jazz band that was structured after Cal Tjader. The leader was a vibraphone player, the percussionist was Jerry Gonzalez of Fort Apache fame and his brother Andy Gonzalez. It was at the Music and Art High School in New York. And so I was at that band and at the same time I was working with one of my first mentors named Leroy Kirkland, who wrote “Cloudburst,” I don’t know if you know that tune.

He wrote “Cloudburst,” and he was also the arranger of a famous R&B tune called “Our Day Will Come,” Ruby and the Romantics. So I became kind of his protégé. Because his son felt I should meet his father. And he lived right down the block from the school, so a lot of times after, instead of going home I’d go to his house. And he’d have me rehearsing with some of the singers that would come by the crib, he took me to sessions, I met Kenny Burrell through him, I met Jerome Richardson through him, because he was doing a lot of studio work, so all these guys in the studio. So I was in this whole world of these big guys you know. So again, with the big band — well the big band also — the Latin jazz band, doing duos, four hand piano with another keyboard player in the school, and doing the R&B thing, it just again contributed to this whole eclectic approach and love for all styles of music.
